messages.body_plain:
Thanks Perry for your reply. The command Vw[,] <- M[1:n,1:n] is redundant. I removed it from both the models and the problem persists.

The two models are exactly same because in the first model I create Vw = some matrix/sigma then define G= chol(inverse(t(Vw)%*%Vw) = whereas in the second model instead of dividing Vw by sigma first I directly define G= sigma*chol(inverse(t(Vw)%*%Vw)). So the operations are commutative.

I have also seen poor convergence of sigma in multivariate models but that is not my concern here. Its the radically different convergence of sigma for two models that differ by the order in which I divide/multiply by sigma that bothers me because the results are very different and I dont know which model to use. On this note, I should mention that there was a third equivalent version where the w's were specified sequentially instead of jointly. This sequential univariate version was also equivalent to the first two models but again had very poor convergence. I didn't add the code and results to avoid confusion.

> Can you clarify what you intend for Vw? >
> I haven’t checked the math on whether those should be equivalent models, but purely in terms of the code, I think the placement of sigma should be ok either way.
>

>

>
> That pattern of (poor) mixing for a standard deviation is not uncommon.  One simple trick that can help is to include a sampler that operates on a log scale.  Simply add a univariate random walk with “log = TRUE” in the control list. The qualitative appearance of the mixing of the sigmas does not look wildly different to me.  The top one gets entrained near zero for some of the later iterations.  But is that a truly different mixing regime or just a different stochastic realization?

One way you could check would be to set the inits and use set.seed from R to set the random number seed.  Then you could look at the samplers (mcmcConf$printSamplers()) to make sure that the slight change in how the model is written has not changed the order of the samplers (which could validly happen).  Assuming the samplers are in the same order (and you could reorder them if needed with mcmcConf$setSamplers) you could run each for a short number of iterations and see if they do exactly the same thing, starting from the same inits and the same seed.  Of course there may be numerical rounding differences in the two models but for a short number of iterations that doesn’t seem likely to lead to different MCMC results.  Is that the kind of diagnostic you are looking for?  If something is wrong, I think that would help us pin it down.

Perry

> The qualitative appearance of the mixing of the sigmas does not look wildly different to me.  The top one gets entrained near zero for some of the later iterations.  But is that a truly different mixing regime or just a different stochastic realization?

> One way you could check would be to set the inits and use set.seed from R to set the random number seed.  Then you could look at the samplers (mcmcConf$printSamplers()) to make sure that the slight change in how the model is written has not changed the order of the samplers (which could validly happen).  Assuming the samplers are in the same order (and you could reorder them if needed with mcmcConf$setSamplers) you could run each for a short number of iterations and see if they do exactly the same thing, starting from the same inits and the same seed.  Of course there may be numerical rounding differences in the two models but for a short number of iterations that doesn’t seem likely to lead to different MCMC results.  Is that the kind of diagnostic you are looking for?  If something is wrong, I think that would help us pin it down.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Abhirup, here's what is happening.

In the 6th iteration, a negative sigma is proposed. In model 1, this
produces a positive valued G, and the proposal is rejected because of the
-Inf log probability for sigma. In model 2, this produces a negative valued
G, and the proposal is rejected but based on a -Inf log probability for
sigma and an NaN log probability for w. Because of the NaN, there is a
slightly different set of calculations done, and the result is a shift by
one value in what random numbers are used subsequently in the MCMCs for the
two models. So then you get different stochastic realizations from the
posterior.

I agree with Perry that I don't see the two chains as really differing so
it's not the case that one is the 'correct' one to use. Both show poor
mixing and model 1 seems to get stuck, but if you run model 2 longer, I
suspect it would get similarly stuck at times.

If you use the 'log' option for the sigma parameter RW sampler (or the
'reflective' option), you shouldn't see this occur, because negative sigma
values won't ever be proposed. But that is just tidying up a numerical
anomaly, not changing the substance of the issue, which is the slow mixing.

For future reference for anyone reading this, I diagnosed this by running
the _uncompiled_ version of the MCMC, using debug(onedagarMCMC1$run) function
and stepping through the MCMC code.

-Chris

> Hi Abhirup, here's what is happening.
>
> In the 6th iteration, a negative sigma is proposed. In model 1, this
> produces a positive valued G, and the proposal is rejected because of the
> -Inf log probability for sigma. In model 2, this produces a negative valued
> G, and the proposal is rejected but based on a -Inf log probability for
> sigma and an NaN log probability for w. Because of the NaN, there is a
> slightly different set of calculations done, and the result is a shift by
> one value in what random numbers are used subsequently in the MCMCs for the
> two models. So then you get different stochastic realizations from the
> posterior.

> it's not the case that one is the 'correct' one to use. Both show poor
> mixing and model 1 seems to get stuck, but if you run model 2 longer, I
> suspect it would get similarly stuck at times.
>
> If you use the 'log' option for the sigma parameter RW sampler (or the
> 'reflective' option), you shouldn't see this occur, because negative sigma
> values won't ever be proposed. But that is just tidying up a numerical
> anomaly, not changing the substance of the issue, which is the slow mixing.

> the _uncompiled_ version of the MCMC, using debug(onedagarMCMC1$run) function

Hi,

The following two models are equivalent but are giving different dependency graphs (and hence very different results using MCMC). Any insight on why this is happening will be very helpful.

Thanks,
Abhi

library(nimble)

onedagarCode <- nimbleCode({
    w[1] ~ dnorm(0, invsigmasq)
    y[1] ~ dnorm(inprod(X[1, 1:p], beta[1:p]) + w[1], invtausq)
    for (i in 2:n){
        weight <- rho/(1+(dni[i-1]-1)*rho^2)

        mw <- w[i-1]
        w[i] ~ dnorm(mw*weight, invsigmasq*(1+(dni[i-1]-1)*rho^2)/(1-rho^2))     #### difference with the second model, mw is specified first and then used in the mean of w[i]

        y[i] ~ dnorm(inprod(X[i, 1:p], beta[1:p]) + w[i], invtausq)
    }
    beta[] ~ dmnorm(mubeta[],cholesky=Cbeta[,], prec_param=0)
    invsigmasq ~ dgamma(2, rate=1)
    invtausq ~ dgamma(2, rate=0.2)
    rho ~dunif(0,1)
})

    w[1] ~ dnorm(0, invsigmasq)
    y[1] ~ dnorm(inprod(X[1, 1:p], beta[1:p]) + w[1], invtausq)

        w[i] ~ dnorm(w[i-1]*weight, invsigmasq*(1+(dni[i-1]-1)*rho^2)/(1-rho^2))     #### difference with the first model, mean of w[i] is specified directly

        y[i] ~ dnorm(inprod(X[i, 1:p], beta[1:p]) + w[i], invtausq)
    }
    beta[] ~ dmnorm(mubeta[],cholesky=Cbeta[,], prec_param=0)
    invsigmasq ~ dgamma(2, rate=1)
    invtausq ~ dgamma(2, rate=0.2)
    rho ~dunif(0,1)

Hi Gil,

I think there are a couple of things going on here.

First, you are running into NIMBLE’s need for static types when compiling.  Specifically, you have created sgamma as a matrix, so it must remain a matrix.  When you do sgamma <- gamma[j-1,2:n], you are assigning a vector into a matrix, which is causing a problem.  Mimicking R, NIMBLE allows gamma[j-1, 2:n, drop = FALSE] so it will return a matrix instead of a vector, which you should be able to assign to a matrix.  (drop = FALSE means it will not drop a dimension due to the single index).  Another way to do it would be sgamma[1, 1:size] <- vector

Second, the current release of NIMBLE does not support c().  You have two choices.  c() and a variety of other core R features are supported on the devel branch of our github repository.  So if you want you can install nimble from there (library(devtools); install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "devel", subdir = "packages/nimble”).  Still the c() will return a vector so you would have to assign into a vector.  Another option (without installing from devel) is to assign into each piece of sgamma by a separate line instead of using c() to do it in one line.

Looks like the same issues may come up for some of your other variables.

Perry
